digest.top_line: NRG-GY020: adding 1y pembro to adjuvant VBT ± EBRT did not improve RFS3 (73% vs 70%, p=0.68) in early-stage HIR dMMR EC; G3/4 tox 43% vs 15%.
digest.tldr: RT stays the adjuvant backbone in early-stage HIR dMMR endometrioid EC: pembro added toxicity, not RFS (sources conflict on the RT+pembro rate). EORTC 1420 Best-of: no 12-mo MDADI difference, TOS vs DO-IMRT in T1-2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC (+3.9, p=0.326), more mucosal toxicity with RT. FCCSS: MLD 5-10 Gy → SPLC sHR 3.75 in childhood survivors.

studies.name: FCCSS second primary lung cancer risk in childhood cancer survivors
studies.tldr: Mean lung dose 5-10 Gy carried sHR 3.75 (1.44-9.78) for second primary lung cancer; CIF 6.50% at age 60 vs 1.79% non-irradiated.
details: 🔍 French Childhood Cancer Survivors Study: 7,006 5-year CCS, median f/u 34.1 yr (IQR 27.2-42.2)
🔍 Individual MLD reconstructed by phantom-based dosimetry; Fine-Gray competing-risk models
📊 46 SPLCs, median age at dx 50.3 yr; adenocarcinoma 44%
📊 SIR 2.26 (95% CI 1.65-3.01) vs French general population

details.text: 📐 Multivariable SPLC risk factors (n=5,760 with smoking data; 42 SPLCs)

details: 📊 MLD 5-10 Gy: 5% of cohort, 21% of SPLC cases

subdetails: MLD >5 Gy survivors: 66.7% of SPLC cases attributable to RT

details: ⚠️ Risk estimates for MLD bands >10 Gy not reported in source
⚠️ Screening benefit itself not tested; guideline proposal extrapolated from risk data

verdict.rationale: Retrospective cohort, abstract only, 46 events; dose threshold derived from small subgroup and screening benefit in CCS never tested prospectively.
verdict.audience: Adult 5-year childhood cancer survivors, esp. prior thoracic RT

studies.significance: The risk peak sits at a modest MLD of 5-10 Gy, a band that covers only 5% of survivors yet 21% of cases, and among MLD >5 Gy survivors 66.7% of SPLCs were attributable to RT. That makes reconstructed MLD, not just a yes/no history of thoracic RT, the variable to carry into survivorship referral. Risk above 10 Gy is not reported in the source.
studies.monday_clinic: In an adult childhood cancer survivor with prior thoracic RT and MLD >5 Gy, this supports discussing earlier LDCT screening; it does not show screening benefit in this group and adds no signal for chemotherapy-only survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Cohort analysis of the **French Childhood Cancer Survivors Study**, SPLCs confirmed histopathologically across multiple data sources. **Median follow-up 34.1 years**. SIRs vs the French general population; Fine-Gray competing-risk models adjusted for sex, age, diagnosis period and smoking.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **7,006 5-year childhood cancer survivors**. Multivariable models restricted to the **5,760 with complete smoking data** (42 SPLCs).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Individual **mean lung dose reconstructed with phantom-based dosimetry**. SPLC cases more often had prior thoracic irradiation (41% vs 19%).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall **SIR 2.26** (1.65-3.01). **MLD 5-10 Gy sHR 3.75** (1.44-9.78), with CIF 6.50% at age 60 vs 1.79% non-irradiated. Smoking sHR 2.57; prior chemotherapy **not significant**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: LDCT screening evidence such as NLST and NELSON comes from tobacco-exposed adults, not irradiated survivors. This cohort supplies a dose-based risk signal for a population those trials did not address, without testing screening itself.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adult survivors of childhood cancer treated in historical eras with reconstructed thoracic RT dose. Does not represent survivors treated with modern conformal or proton techniques, or adult-onset cancer survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Phantom-based dose reconstruction carries uncertainty for historical fields. Smoking data incomplete for part of the cohort, and **risk above 10 Gy MLD not reported in source**, so dose-response shape is unclear.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data argue for stratifying survivorship screening by MLD rather than RT exposure alone. Start age, interval and mortality benefit of LDCT in this group remain unsettled.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The risk peak sits at MLD 5-10 Gy (sHR 3.75), so low-dose lung bath counts, not only high-dose volume. For survivorship clinics, a reconstructed MLD >5 Gy flags the group where 66.7% of SPLCs were RT-attributable; bands above 10 Gy are not reported in source.

open_questions: Does LDCT screening reduce lung cancer mortality in irradiated childhood cancer survivors?
Optimal screening start age by mean lung dose band
Does SPLC risk persist with modern conformal or proton pediatric RT?

sites.intro: Randomised phase III test of adding IO to the adjuvant RT backbone in dMMR early-stage endometrial cancer.

studies.name: NRG-GY020
studies.tldr: Adding 1y pembrolizumab to adjuvant VBT ± EBRT did not improve RFS3 (73% RT vs 70% RT+pembro, p=0.68) in early-stage HIR dMMR endometrioid EC; G3/4 toxicity 43% vs 15%.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase III open-label superiority trial, 2:1, N=168 (112 RT+pembro vs 56 RT), enrolled 2/2020-8/2022
🔍 Newly diagnosed early-stage HIR (GOG-249 criteria) dMMR endometrioid EC; stage IA 20%, IB 63%, II 17%; 82% grade 2/3

details.text: 🩻 RT backbone identical in both arms
subdetails: EBRT allowed only for stage II and IB grade 3

details: 💊 Pembrolizumab 400 mg IV q6w × 1y, started within 7 days of RT

details.text: 📊 Outcomes by arm, median f/u 45.5 mo

details: ⚠️ Sources conflict on the primary result: abstract 70% vs OncLive's presentation report 77% for RT+pembro; failure counts also differ

details.text: ⚠️ Primary endpoint counts any off-study pt as a failure, which penalizes the more toxic open-label arm
subdetails: Abstract: non-recurrence failures 5 (9%) RT vs 22 (20%) RT+pembro
OncLive: unknown-status failures 5 (9%) RT vs 14 (13%) RT+pembro
OncLive: consent withdrawals 3 RT vs 12 RT+pembro

details: ⚠️ Small N for a phase III; KM HR CI 0.33-1.61 cannot exclude a meaningful recurrence benefit or harm
⚠️ Excess G3/4 toxicity mostly G3 lymphopenia and hypertension
🔗 Eligibility built on GOG-249 HIR criteria; OncLive cites GOG 249 3y RFS 82% and 18% distant recurrence in HIR disease

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase III failed prespecified superiority with higher G3/4 toxicity, reaffirming RT alone. Small N, open-label, and a withdrawal-sensitive composite primary limit precision.
verdict.audience: Newly diagnosed early-stage HIR dMMR endometrioid EC, post-surgery

studies.significance: Raw recurrences ran 18% with RT alone vs 11% with RT+pembro, but the primary endpoint scored withdrawals as failures, and withdrawals clustered in the open-label pembro arm. For the RT reader, VBT ± EBRT stays the complete adjuvant answer for HIR dMMR disease; whether IO lowers recurrence on top of VBT remains untested at adequate power.
studies.monday_clinic: In newly diagnosed early-stage HIR dMMR endometrioid EC after surgery, this does not support adding pembrolizumab to adjuvant VBT ± EBRT; it does not address advanced or recurrent dMMR disease, where IO activity is established.

primary_endpoint.name: 3-year recurrence-free survival proportion (RFS3)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: RT vs RT+pembro, p=0.68 (abstract); OncLive: 73% vs 77%, P=.3057

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase III open-label superiority** trial, 2:1, **N=168** enrolled 2/2020-8/2022. Median follow-up **45.5 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Newly diagnosed **early-stage HIR (GOG-249 criteria) dMMR endometrioid EC**. Median age 66; stage IA 20%, IB 63%, II 17%; 82% grade 2/3.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **VBT in all pts**; EBRT permitted only for stage II and IB grade 3. 70% received VBT alone and 30% EBRT ± VBT. Dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Pembrolizumab 400 mg IV q6w for 1y**, starting within 7 days of RT, vs RT alone.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** proportion recurrence-free at 3y (RFS3), with recurrence, death, or coming off study before 3y all counted as failure. Secondary: log-rank, Cox models, KM comparisons at 3y.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3/4 toxicity **43% vs 15%** with pembro, mostly G3 lymphopenia and hypertension.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: VBT as the adjuvant standard for HIR EC is the reference practice this trial tried to build on; GOG-249 defined the HIR population, with OncLive citing its **82%** 3y RFS. IO activity in recurrent dMMR EC did not transfer to the early-stage adjuvant setting here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents newly diagnosed early-stage HIR dMMR endometrioid EC receiving adjuvant VBT ± EBRT. Does not represent pMMR, non-endometrioid, or advanced/recurrent dMMR EC.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Abstract and OncLive's presentation report give **different RFS3 values for the pembro arm (70% vs 77%)** and different failure counts. Withdrawals (12 vs 3 consent withdrawals per OncLive) drive the primary endpoint, and recurrence site patterns are not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Recurrence counts and KM RFS lean toward pembro, but the HR CI 0.33-1.61 spans no effect, and 3y OS was **96% in both arms**. With tripled G3/4 toxicity and no survival signal, **RT alone remains the standard**; a benefit in recurrence prevention is not excluded but is not shown.

studies.interpretation:
NRG-GY020 asked a reasonable biological question: dMMR is the strongest predictive biomarker for checkpoint inhibitor activity in recurrent endometrial cancer, so why not move pembrolizumab into the adjuvant setting for early-stage disease at elevated risk? The answer at this sample size is that the trial cannot show it helps, and it clearly adds toxicity. That combination is enough to keep VBT with or without EBRT as the complete adjuvant treatment for the GOG-249-defined HIR dMMR endometrioid population, which is what the investigators concluded.

The more interesting problem is the primary endpoint. RFS3 was scored as a proportion in which coming off study for any reason before 3 years counted as failure. In an open-label trial where one arm carries a year of q6w infusions and G3/4 toxicity of 43% vs 15%, that design will predictably tilt against the experimental arm, because the burdened pts are the ones who withdraw. The source data fit that pattern: recurrences were 10/56 (18%) with RT and 12/112 (11%) with RT+pembro, while non-recurrence failures went the other way. The KM analysis, which handles withdrawal by censoring rather than counting it as failure, gave RFS 81% vs 88% and HR 0.72 with a 95% CI of 0.33 to 1.61. A reader should not take that as a hidden positive; the interval is wide enough to include harm, and censoring is only unbiased if withdrawal is unrelated to recurrence risk, which is untestable here. But it does mean the null primary is partly a statement about tolerability and retention, not only about efficacy.

The sources also disagree on the headline number, which should lower confidence in any single figure. The abstract reports RFS3 70% for RT+pembro with Z=-0.48, p=0.68 and 22 non-recurrence failures; OncLive's account of the presentation reports 77% with Z=0.508, P=.3057 and 14 unknown-status failures, 12 of them consent withdrawals. The most plausible explanation is an updated data cut or reclassified failures between abstract and podium, but the source does not say. Either version fails superiority, so the conclusion holds; what changes is whether the pembro arm looks numerically worse or slightly better on the primary.

For radiation oncologists, the RT backbone was held constant and was the standard one: VBT for everyone, EBRT reserved for stage II and IB grade 3, with 70% receiving VBT alone. Nothing here argues for changing RT volume or adding EBRT, and nothing suggests IO compensates for omitting RT, since that was never tested. The missing piece is the pattern of failure. The rationale for adding a systemic agent to VBT was the extravaginal and distant recurrence risk of dMMR HIR disease that OncLive described, yet the source does not report where recurrences occurred. Without vaginal versus pelvic versus distant breakdown, one cannot tell whether pembro was acting on the failure mode it was meant to address.

With 3y OS at 96% in both arms and excellent outcomes overall, the bar for accepting a year of immunotherapy and its toxicity in this population is high, and this trial does not clear it. A larger trial with a time-to-event primary, or one restricted to a higher-risk dMMR subset, would be needed to settle whether the recurrence signal is real.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: VBT for all pts, EBRT only for stage II and IB grade 3, and 70% got VBT alone: that backbone stays the complete adjuvant answer for HIR dMMR endometrioid EC. Recurrence site patterns are not reported, so whether IO would have reduced extravaginal failure on top of VBT is unanswered.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: dMMR status alone did not justify 1y adjuvant pembrolizumab after RT: RFS3 missed superiority and G3/4 toxicity rose to 43% vs 15%. Raw recurrences (11% vs 18%) and KM HR 0.72 (0.33-1.61) leave a possible signal that this trial was too small to confirm.

open_questions: Does adjuvant IO reduce extravaginal recurrence in higher-risk dMMR subsets?
Recurrence patterns (vaginal vs distant) by arm not reported
Would a time-to-event primary endpoint have changed the result?

sites.intro: Randomised TOS vs DO-IMRT in early oropharynx/supraglottis/hypopharynx: swallowing function comparable, toxicity profiles differ.

studies.name: EORTC 1420 Best-of
studies.tldr: 12-mo MDADI adjusted difference +3.9 points (90%CI -2.7 to +10.5; p=0.326), TOS vs DO-IMRT; no swallowing difference, more mucosal toxicity with DO-IMRT.
details: 📊 Primary endpoint MDADI total at 12 mo: adjusted difference +3.9 points (90%CI -2.7 to +10.5; p=0.326)
📊 Adjusted MDADI differences at 4.5, 6 and 9 mo: +6.6, +4.2 and +3.5
🔍 Phase III, 1:1, 86 randomised (42 TOS, 44 DO-IMRT), 25 centres, 9 countries, 2018-2024

subdetails: T1/T2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC or T1 N0 HPSCC, suitable for either modality

details.text: 📊 Treatment-related AEs (all grades), TOS vs DO-IMRT

details: ⚠️ 7/44 (16%) allocated to DO-IMRT declined treatment; all TOS pts had surgery
⚠️ 12-mo MDADI evaluable in 74% overall: 86% TOS vs 64% DO-IMRT
⚠️ 90%CI upper bound +10.5 does not exclude the 10-point difference the trial was powered for
⚠️ DO-IMRT dose, fractionation and constraints not reported in source
🔗 Consistent in direction with ORATOR (randomised TORS vs RT in OPSCC): function comparable, toxicity profiles differ

verdict.rationale: Phase III, but differential 12-mo MDADI evaluability (86% vs 64%) and 16% refusal of DO-IMRT; CI does not exclude the 10-point margin, so equivalence is not shown.
verdict.audience: T1-T2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC or T1 N0 HPSCC, fit for TOS or RT

studies.significance: The RT cost is mucosal, not swallowing: DO-IMRT carried mucositis 39% vs 10%, dry mouth 49% vs 14% and dysgeusia 46% vs 17%, against TOS hemorrhage 5% and fistula 2%, with G≥3 TRAEs 21% each. DO-IMRT dose, fractionation and target volume are not reported in source, so dysphagia-sparing constraints cannot be benchmarked.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1/T2 N0-1 oropharyngeal or supraglottic, or T1 N0 hypopharyngeal carcinoma fit for either modality, this supports choosing TOS or DO-IMRT on toxicity profile and preference rather than expected 12-month swallowing; it does not address T3-T4 or N2+ disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III**, randomised 1:1, 25 centres in 9 countries, accrual 2018-2024. Powered (80%, **alpha 10% two-sided**) for a **10-point** MDADI difference; 54 evaluable needed, 84 planned for 35% attrition, **86 randomised**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1/T2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC or T1 N0 HPSCC** suitable for either TOS or DO-IMRT. Median age 64, 86% OPSCC, 49% HPV-positive; arms balanced.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Dysphagia-optimized IMRT (DO-IMRT). **Dose, fractionation and target volumes not reported in source.** 7/44 (16%) allocated to DO-IMRT declined treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** MDADI total score at 12 months (ANCOVA). Secondary: MDADI at 4.5, 6 and 9 months, PSS-HN, oncological outcomes, toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 12-mo MDADI adjusted difference **+3.9 points (90%CI -2.7 to +10.5; p=0.326)**, consistent across sensitivity analyses. Arm-level secondary outcomes are in the table.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G≥3 treatment-related AEs **21% in each arm**. TOS: hemorrhage 5%, fistula 2%. DO-IMRT vs TOS: **mucositis 39% vs 10%, dry mouth 49% vs 14%, dysgeusia 46% vs 17%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ORATOR randomised TORS against RT in OPSCC and also found comparable function with different toxicity profiles. Best-of extends the comparison to **supraglottic and hypopharyngeal** primaries and to a phase III frame, but still with a small N.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1/T2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC or T1 N0 HPSCC suitable for either TOS or DO-IMRT. Does not represent T3-T4 or N2+ disease, or pts not suitable for transoral resection.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The EFS HR CI (0.77-3.50) is wide and follow-up reaches only 2 years. A 49% HPV-positive mix limits transfer to HPV-positive de-escalation. RT technique is unreported, so the DO-IMRT arm cannot be audited.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: With swallowing function apparently similar, **toxicity profile and patient preference** become the deciding factors. The numerically lower CR and EFS in the DO-IMRT arm (98% vs 82%; 84% vs 72%) are not significant and may partly reflect pts who declined RT, so they need longer follow-up before they carry weight.

studies.interpretation:
Best-of is the first phase III to randomise transoral surgery against dysphagia-optimized IMRT in early oropharyngeal, supraglottic and hypopharyngeal carcinoma with swallowing as the primary question. It ends roughly where ORATOR, the earlier randomised oropharyngeal comparison, left the field: no functional reason at 12 months to prefer one modality. The size of what was actually excluded matters, though. The adjusted MDADI difference of +3.9 points has a 90% CI of -2.7 to +10.5, and that upper bound sits just past the 10-point difference the trial was powered to detect. This is a non-significant superiority test at a lenient two-sided alpha of 10%, not a demonstration of equivalence, and reading it as 'swallowing is the same' claims more than the design supports.

The larger methodological problem is who is missing. Twelve-month MDADI was evaluable in 86% of the TOS arm against 64% of the DO-IMRT arm, and 7 of 44 pts allocated to DO-IMRT declined treatment. Missingness that is unequal and tied to refusing the allocated modality is unlikely to be random. The source does not say what the refusers received or whether they contributed MDADI data, so the DO-IMRT estimate rests on a smaller and possibly selected group. The investigators frame the refusal rate as evidence of how hard equipoise is to hold. For anyone designing the next surgery-versus-RT trial in this space, that may be the most transferable finding.

The oncologic secondaries lean toward TOS in raw terms: CR at 6 months 98% vs 82%, 2-year EFS 84% vs 72% with HR=1.64 and a 95% CI of 0.77-3.50. A trial sized for a functional endpoint has little power here, and the CR gap may partly reflect intention-to-treat accounting of pts who never started RT. Overall survival was 97% with TOS and 100% with DO-IMRT. The honest reading is that nothing oncologic has been shown, but a radiation oncologist should not wave the EFS signal away either. It is the number most worth watching at longer follow-up.

For the RT reader, the toxicity split is the actionable content. DO-IMRT produced the expected mucosal profile, with more mucositis, xerostomia and dysgeusia, while TOS carried hemorrhage and fistula at low rates. Severe treatment-related AEs were 21% in each arm. Because dose, fractionation and constraint details are not reported in the source, it is not possible to judge whether the DO-IMRT arm reflects contemporary constrictor and parotid sparing. The xerostomia and dysgeusia rates therefore cannot be benchmarked against a reader's own practice. The HPV-positive fraction of 49% also places this population between HPV-driven de-escalation cohorts and classic tobacco-related disease, so neither group is cleanly represented.

What the trial changes is the conversation, not the default. For an early-stage pt suitable for either modality, it supports presenting both as functionally comparable at a year, with the choice resting on the type of toxicity the pt would rather risk, tumour characteristics and preference. It does not settle long-term swallowing beyond 12 months, does not establish oncologic equivalence, and says nothing about locally advanced or N2+ disease.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: DO-IMRT's cost is mucosal: mucositis 39% vs 10%, dry mouth 49% vs 14%, dysgeusia 46% vs 17%, with G≥3 TRAEs 21% each. Dose and constraints are not reported in source, and 7/44 declined RT, so the arm's swallowing estimate rests on 64% evaluable.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: All TOS pts were operated, with hemorrhage 5% and fistula 2%. Numerically higher 6-mo CR (98% vs 82%) and 2y EFS (84% vs 72%, HR=1.64, 95%CI 0.77-3.50) are not significant, so oncologic superiority of TOS is not established.

open_questions: Does the EFS gap persist with longer follow-up?
Does HPV status modify the TOS vs RT comparison?

papers.title: Comparable swallowing function at 12 months but divergent toxicity profiles with TOS versus DO-IMRT in early-stage oropharyngeal, supraglottic and hypopharyngeal carcinoma: Primary results of the phase III EORTC 1420 'Best-of' trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1535O · Proffered paper: Head and neck cancer · 2026-10-25 · presented by Christian Simon (Lausanne, Switzerland) · NCT02984410

Background: Early-stage oropharyngeal (OPSCC), supraglottic (SGSCC) and hypopharyngeal (HPSCC) carcinoma achieve comparable cure with TOS or DO-IMRT, yet treatment selection has lacked randomized functional evidence. This phase III trial compared swallowing outcomes between two standards of care in this rare population.
Methods: T1/T2 N0-1 OPSCC/SGSCC or T1 N0 HPSCC patients suitable for TOS or DO-IMRT were randomised 1:1. Primary endpoint: MDADI total score at 12 months (ANCOVA; alpha=10% two-sided; 80% power; 10-point difference). 54 evaluable required; 84 randomised for 35% attrition. Secondary: MDADI at 4.5, 6, 9 months; PSS-HN; oncological outcomes; toxicity.
Results: 86 patients randomised (42 TOS, 44 DO-IMRT) from 25 centres, 9 countries (2018-2024), median age 64 years, 86% OPSCCs, 49% HPV-positive; arms balanced. All TOS patients received surgery; 7/44 (16%) allocated to DO-IMRT declined treatment. 64 patients (74%) had evaluable MDADI at 12 months (86% TOS; 64% DO-IMRT). Mean MDADI: 83.3 (SD 18.3) and 86.2 (SD 15.1); adjusted difference +3.9 points (90%CI: -2.7 to +10.5; p=0.326), consistent across sensitivity analyses. At 4.5, 6 and 9 months, adjusted differences were +6.6, +4.2 and +3.5. At 12 months, PSS-HN: unrestricted diet in 87% (TOS) versus 83% (DO-IMRT); no feeding tube in either arm. Complete response at 6 months: 98% (TOS) versus 82% (DO-IMRT); event-free survival at 2 y 84% (TOS) versus 72% (DO-IMRT) (HR=1.64; 95%CI 0.77-3.50; p=0.200); overall survival 97% (TOS) versus 100% (DO-IMRT). Grade >=3 treatment-related AEs: 21% each; all grades’ treatment-related AEs: TOS: hemorrhage 5%, fistula 2%; DO-IMRT vs TOS: mucositis (39% vs 10%), dry mouth (49% vs 14%) and dysgeusia (46% vs 17%).
Conclusions: No significant difference in swallowing function at 12 months was demonstrated between TOS and DO-IMRT. 16% of patients randomised to DO-IMRT declined treatment, illustrating the challenge of equipoise. Greater mucosal toxicity was observed with DO-IMRT. These findings support individualised treatment selection based on tumour characteristics, patient preference and toxicity profile.
Clinical trial identification: EORTC Protocol Number: 1420, NCT02984410.

papers.title: NRG-GY020: Phase III randomized trial of radiation +/- MK-3475 (pembrolizumab) for newly diagnosed early-stage high intermediate risk (HIR) mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) endometrioid endometrial cancer
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1239O · Proffered paper: Gynaecological cancers · 2026-10-24 · presented by Floor Backes (Columbus, United States of America) · NCT04214067

Background: Currently, vaginal brachytherapy (VBT) is recommended as adjuvant therapy for HIR EC. Immunotherapy (IO) is highly effective for patients with recurrent dMMR EC. We hypothesized that the addition of IO to radiation (RT) would improve recurrence free survival (RFS) in early stage dMMR EC.
Methods: NRG-GY020 was a randomized, phase III open-label superiority trial and included patients with newly diagnosed, early-stage, HIR (GOG-249 criteria), dMMR endometrioid EC. Patients in both arms received VBT; only patients with stage II and IB grade 3 were allowed to receive external beam pelvic radiation (EBRT). Patients were randomized 2:1 to 1 year of pembrolizumab 400 mg IV every 6 weeks starting within 7 days of RT, vs RT alone. The primary analysis compared the proportion of RFS at 3 years (RFS3) between RT+pembro and RT using normal approximations. Patients who reached RFS3 were considered treatment successes, whereas patients who recurred or died of any cause or who came off study within 3 years for any other reason were considered treatment failures. Secondary analyses included a log-rank test, Cox proportional hazards models, and Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves with comparisons at 3 years.
Results: Between 2/2020-8/2022, 168 patients were enrolled. Median age was 66, 77% were white; 20% had stage IA, 63% IB, 17% stage II, with 82% grade 2/3 EC. Most patients (70%) received VBT alone, while 30% received EBRT +/- VBT. The RT+pembro arm experienced more grade 3/4 toxicity (43% vs 15%), mostly grade 3 lymphopenia and hypertension. At data cutoff (median follow up 45.5 months), the standardized statistic comparing the two proportions was Z=-0.48 (p=0.68). RFS3 was 73% for RT vs 70% for RT+pembro; 10/56 (18%) recurrences in the RT and 12/112 (11%) in the RT+pembro arm, and 5 (9%) and 22 (20%) failures for other reasons, respectively. KM estimated RFS was 81% in the RT vs 88% in the RT+ pembro arm (HR 0.72 (95%CI 0.33,1.61; p=0.21). 3-year overall survival (OS) was 96% in both arms.
Conclusions: The addition of pembrolizumab to RT did not meet the pre-specified criteria for superiority. RT alone (VBT and/or EBRT) remains the standard in HIR dMMR endometrioid EC.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04214067.

papers.title: Second primary lung cancer risk in childhood cancer survivors from the FCCSS cohort: Risk-adapted screening guidelines
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 1149RO · Rapid oral: Prevention, early detection and intervention · 2026-10-26 · presented by Pamela Abdayem (Villejuif, France)

Background: Low-dose chest CT (LDCT) screening reduces lung cancer (LC) mortality in high-risk tobacco-exposed individuals. Prior thoracic irradiation is an additional risk factor for LC, but specific dosimetric predictors remain poorly characterized in adult childhood cancer survivors (CCS), limiting tailored screening strategies.
Methods: We analyzed 7,006 5-year CCS from the French Childhood Cancer Survivors Study (FCCSS). Second Primary LCs (SPLCs) were identified through multiple data sources with histopathological confirmation. Individual mean lung doses (MLD) were reconstructed using phantom-based dosimetry. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) were estimated compared to the French general population. Risk factors were assessed using multivariable Fine–Gray competing-risk models and adjusted for sex, age and period of diagnosis, and smoking status. Adjusted cumulative incidence (CIF) and population attributable fraction (PAF) for MLD >5 Gy were estimated.
Results: After a median follow-up of 34.1 years (IQR: 27.2–42.2), 46 SPLCs were identified (median age at diagnosis 50.3 years [IQR: 41.4–54.5]), predominantly adenocarcinomas (44%). Compared to CCS without SPLC, those with SPLC were more frequently survivors of lymphoma (28% vs 17%) and bone sarcoma (15% vs 9%) and were more likely to have undergone prior thoracic irradiation (41% vs. 19%). Overall, CCS had more than a two-fold higher risk compared with the general population (SIR 2.26; 95%CI: 1.65–3.01). Multivariable analyses were restricted to CCS with complete smoking data (n=5,760; 42 SPLCs). A MLD of 5-10 Gy was associated with the highest SPLC risk (sHR 3.75;[1.44–9.78]; p<0.01), accounting for 21% of cases despite representing only 5% overall. Their CIF reached 6.50% at age 60, vs 1.79% in non-irradiated survivors. Smoking was a significant risk factor (2.57 [1.40–4.71], p<0.01), while prior chemotherapy showed no significant association. Among survivors with MLD >5 Gy, 66.7% of SPLC cases were attributable to radiotherapy, vs 23.9% in the overall cohort.
Conclusions: These findings support integrating dosimetric thresholds into risk-adapted LDCT screening guidelines for CCS. Earlier initiation of LDCT screening should be considered for CCS.
